title.en: Systems of Linear Differential Equations, Phase Plane Topology & Matrix Exponentials

body.en: Most realistic mechanical, ecological, and chemical systems consist of interconnected components whose states evolve simultaneously — such as predator-prey populations, multi-loop electrical networks, coupled harmonic oscillators, or satellite orbital attitudes. These multi-dimensional dynamics are modeled by systems of linear differential equations \( \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x} \). This chapter bridges linear algebra and dynamical systems, exploring the eigenvalue-eigenvector method, geometric phase portraits, the trace-determinant classification, and the matrix exponential \( e^{At} \).

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Definition 7.1: First-Order Linear Systems & Phase Space

body.en: A system of two first-order linear homogeneous differential equations with constant coefficients is written in matrix-vector form: \[ \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = A\mathbf{x}, \qquad \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1(t) \\ x_2(t) \end{pmatrix}, \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. \] The \( x_1 x_2 \)-plane is called the phase plane. At each point \( \mathbf{x} \), the matrix product \( A\mathbf{x} \) defines a velocity vector \( \mathbf{x}' \), establishing a continuous direction field. A curve \( \mathbf{x}(t) \) tangent to this field at every instant is a trajectory (orbit), and the complete geometric collection of trajectories is the phase portrait.

label.en: ▲ Level 1 Foundation — Theorem 7.1: Eigenpairs & Fundamental Solution Sets

body.en:
Substituting the exponential ansatz \( \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} \) into \( \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x} \) yields: \[ \lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} = A(e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}) = e^{\lambda t} A\mathbf{v} \iff A\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}. \] Thus \( \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} \) is a non-trivial solution if and only if \( \lambda \) is an eigenvalue of \( A \) with associated non-zero eigenvector \( \mathbf{v} \).

If \( A \) has two distinct real eigenvalues \( \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 \) with linearly independent eigenvectors \( \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \), the general solution is: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = C_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1 + C_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2. \]

Since \( A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1 \), \( \frac{d}{dt}[e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1] = \lambda_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1 = e^{\lambda_1 t} A\mathbf{v}_1 = A(e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1) \), satisfying the system. Linear combinations satisfy the system by linearity of matrix multiplication: \[ \frac{d}{dt}[C_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + C_2 \mathbf{x}_2] = C_1 \mathbf{x}_1' + C_2 \mathbf{x}_2' = C_1 A\mathbf{x}_1 + C_2 A\mathbf{x}_2 = A(C_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + C_2 \mathbf{x}_2). \] Because \( \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 \), their eigenvectors \( \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \) are linearly independent in \( \mathbb{R}^2 \). The Wronskian \( W(t) = \det[e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1 \quad e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2] = e^{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t}\det[\mathbf{v}_1 \quad \mathbf{v}_2] \neq 0 \), proving that every initial vector \( \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{x}_0 \) can be uniquely represented.

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — Theorem 7.2: Trace-Determinant Plane & Phase Portrait Topology

body.en:
The eigenvalues of \( A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \) are the roots of the characteristic equation \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - \tau \lambda + \Delta = 0, \] where \( \tau = \operatorname{tr}(A) = a + d \) and \( \Delta = \det(A) = ad - bc \). The discriminant is \( D = \tau^2 - 4\Delta \). The topological classification of the equilibrium point at the origin \( (0, 0) \) is completely determined by \( (\tau, \Delta) \):

  • Saddle Point (\( \Delta < 0 \)): Eigenvalues are real with opposite signs (\( \lambda_1 > 0 > \lambda_2 \)). Always unstable. Trajectories approach along the eigenvector direction of \( \lambda_2 < 0 \) and escape along the direction of \( \lambda_1 > 0 \).
  • Nodal Sink / Stable Node (\( \Delta > 0, D > 0, \tau < 0 \)): Real negative eigenvalues (\( \lambda_2 < \lambda_1 < 0 \)). All trajectories converge to origin tangentially to \( \mathbf{v}_1 \). Asymptotically stable.
  • Nodal Source / Unstable Node (\( \Delta > 0, D > 0, \tau > 0 \)): Real positive eigenvalues (\( \lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > 0 \)). All trajectories diverge to infinity. Unstable.
  • Spiral Sink (\( \Delta > 0, D < 0, \tau < 0 \)): Complex roots \( \lambda = \alpha \pm i\beta \) with \( \alpha < 0 \). Trajectories spiral inward to origin. Asymptotically stable.
  • Spiral Source (\( \Delta > 0, D < 0, \tau > 0 \)): Complex roots with \( \alpha > 0 \). Trajectories spiral outward. Unstable.
  • Center (\( \Delta > 0, D < 0, \tau = 0 \)): Purely imaginary roots \( \lambda = \pm i\beta \). Trajectories form closed concentric ellipses. Neutrally stable.

label.en: Worked example 7.A — Saddle Point & Stable/Unstable Manifolds

body.en:
Find the general solution and classify the phase portrait for \[ \mathbf{x}' = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}. \]

Step 1: Characteristic polynomial: \[ \det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 - \lambda & 1 \\ 4 & -2 - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (1 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 + \lambda - 6 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda + 3) = 0. \] Eigenvalues: \( \lambda_1 = 2 \) (positive), \( \lambda_2 = -3 \) (negative). Since \( \Delta = -6 < 0 \), the origin is a saddle point.

Step 2: Eigenvectors:
For \( \lambda_1 = 2 \): \[ (A - 2I)\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 4 & -4 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \implies -v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]
For \( \lambda_2 = -3 \): \[ (A + 3I)\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \implies 4v_1 + v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 3: General solution: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = C_1 e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + C_2 e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}. \] The line spanned by \( (1, -4)^T \) is the stable manifold (inflowing as \( t \to \infty \)); the line spanned by \( (1, 1)^T \) is the unstable manifold (outflowing as \( t \to \infty \)).

label.en: Worked example 7.B — Complex Conjugate Eigenvalues & Spiral Sink

body.en:
Solve \( \mathbf{x}' = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x} \), and verify the rotational direction of trajectories.

Step 1: Characteristic polynomial: \[ \det\begin{pmatrix} -1 - \lambda & -4 \\ 1 & -1 - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (\lambda + 1)^2 + 4 = 0 \implies \lambda = -1 \pm 2i. \] Damping \( \alpha = -1 < 0 \implies \) asymptotically stable spiral sink.

Step 2: Complex eigenvector for \( \lambda = -1 + 2i \): \[ (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} -2i & -4 \\ 1 & -2i \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \implies v_1 - 2i v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 2i \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + i \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 3: Decompose into real and imaginary parts: \[ e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v} = e^{-t}(\cos 2t + i\sin 2t)\left[\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + i\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] \] \[ = e^{-t}\left[\cos 2t \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \sin 2t \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] + i e^{-t}\left[\sin 2t \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \cos 2t \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right]. \] Fundamental real solutions: \[ \mathbf{x}_1(t) = e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} -2\sin 2t \\ \cos 2t \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_2(t) = e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 2\cos 2t \\ \sin 2t \end{pmatrix}. \] \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = C_1 e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} -2\sin 2t \\ \cos 2t \end{pmatrix} + C_2 e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 2\cos 2t \\ \sin 2t \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 4: Rotational sense: Test the velocity vector at \( (1, 0) \): \[ \mathbf{x}' = A \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Since \( x_2' = +1 > 0 \), motion is directed upward into the second quadrant, establishing counterclockwise inward spiraling.

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem 7.3: The Matrix Exponential e^(At), Defective Systems & Generalized Eigenvectors

body.en:
1. The Matrix Exponential: For any \( n \times n \) matrix \( A \), the matrix exponential is defined by the absolutely convergent power series: \[ e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^k}{k!} A^k = I + t A + \frac{t^2}{2!} A^2 + \dots \] Differentiating term-by-term yields \( \frac{d}{dt} e^{At} = A e^{At} \). Consequently, the unique solution to the IVP \( \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{x}_0 \) is: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0. \]

2. Cayley-Hamilton Construction: By the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, \( A \) satisfies its own characteristic equation: \( A^2 - \tau A + \Delta I = 0 \). Thus higher powers \( A^k \) reduce linearly to \( A \) and \( I \), enabling exact evaluation of \( e^{At} = a_0(t)I + a_1(t)A \).

3. Defective Systems & Generalized Eigenvectors: When \( A \) has a repeated eigenvalue \( \lambda \) with only one linearly independent eigenvector \( \mathbf{v}_1 \) (algebraic multiplicity 2, geometric multiplicity 1), \( A \) is defective. A second linearly independent solution requires a generalized eigenvector \( \mathbf{v}_2 \) satisfying: \[ (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1. \] The general solution is then given exactly by: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = C_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 + C_2 e^{\lambda t}\big(\mathbf{v}_2 + t\mathbf{v}_1\big). \]

In a saddle equilibrium, trajectories approach along the stable eigenspace and deflect hyperbolically away along the unstable eigenspace, forming distinct topological sectors separated by straight-line separatrices, as shown below.

caption.en: Hyperbolic trajectories of a saddle point. The stable manifold pulls state trajectories inward toward the origin, while the unstable manifold drives trajectories outward to infinity.

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps & University Pitfalls — Defective Eigenvalues & Spiral Direction

body.en:
Incorrect defective ansatz: For a repeated eigenvalue, students often mistakenly write \( C_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 + C_2 t e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 \). Substituting \( t e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 \) gives \( \mathbf{x}' = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 + \lambda t e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 \), but \( A\mathbf{x} = \lambda t e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 \) — leaving an unbalanced \( e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}_1 \)! The correct second term is \( e^{\lambda t}(\mathbf{v}_2 + t\mathbf{v}_1) \) where \( (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 \).

Spiral orientation test: Eigenvalues \( \alpha \pm i\beta \) tell you stability and frequency, but CANNOT tell you whether the spiral turns clockwise or counterclockwise. Always test the velocity vector at \( (1, 0) \): compute \( A \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a \\ c \end{pmatrix} \). If \( c > 0 \), rotation is counterclockwise; if \( c < 0 \), rotation is clockwise.

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Systems of Linear Differential Equations, Phase Plane Topology & Matrix Exponentials (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): The second-order linear homogeneous ODE \( W''(k) - 37W'(k) + 186W(k) = 0 \) has characteristic roots \( \lambda_1, \lambda_2 \). Find the exact value of the trace sum \( \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: From \( \lambda^2 - 37\lambda + 186 = 0 \), the sum of roots is \( 37 \).

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Systems of Linear Differential Equations, Phase Plane Topology & Matrix Exponentials (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): The separable initial value problem \( \dfrac{dW}{dk} = 24k \) satisfies \( W(0) = 13 \). Find the exact value of the solution value \( W(14) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Integrating gives \( W(k) = 12k^2 + 13 \), so \( W(14) = 2365 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Systems of Linear Differential Equations, Phase Plane Topology & Matrix Exponentials)

rows.en: Writing \(\ln|y| = x^2 + C \implies y = e^{x^2} + C\)
Exponentiation distributes over addition as multiplication (\(e^{a+b} = e^a e^b\)), not addition.
Write \(y = e^{x^2 + C} = Ae^{x^2}\) and solve for \(A\) using the initial condition.
Leaving original \(x\)-limits on a \(u\)-substituted definite integral
Evaluates the antiderivative \(F(u)\) at \(x\)-values instead of \(u(x)\)-values.
Convert bounds immediately: \(u_{\text{low}} = u(a)\) and \(u_{\text{high}} = u(b)\).
Cancels forward and backward motion (net displacement) instead of accumulating total path length.
Split the integral at every root where \(v(t) = 0\) and integrate \(|v(t)|\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Systems of Linear Differential Equations, Phase Plane Topology & Matrix Exponentials

body.en: Quick Verification Trick (University Ordinary Differential Equations): For any indefinite integral \(\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C\), differentiate your answer \(F'(x)\) mentally—especially the coefficient \(1/k\) from chain-rule reversal \(\int e^{kx}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{k}e^{kx} + C\)—before moving on.

solution.en:
Step 1: Eigenvalues: \[ \det\begin{pmatrix} 3 - \lambda & -2 \\ 2 & -2 - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (3 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda) + 4 = \lambda^2 - \lambda - 2 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda + 1) = 0. \] \[ \lambda_1 = 2, \qquad \lambda_2 = -1. \]

Step 2: Eigenvectors:
For \( \lambda_1 = 2 \): \( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \implies v_1 - 2v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \).
For \( \lambda_2 = -1 \): \( \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \implies 2v_1 - v_2 = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 3: Apply initial condition \( \mathbf{x}(0) = (3, 1)^T \): \[ C_1 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + C_2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{cases} 2C_1 + C_2 = 3 \\ C_1 + 2C_2 = 1 \end{cases} \] Multiplying second equation by 2 and subtracting: \( 3C_1 = 5 \implies C_1 = 5/3 \), \( C_2 = 1 - 2(5/3) = -7/3 \).

Step 4: Particular solution: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \frac{5}{3}e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{7}{3}e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{10}{3}e^{2t} - \frac{7}{3}e^{-t} \\ \frac{5}{3}e^{2t} - \frac{14}{3}e^{-t} \end{pmatrix}. \]

solution.en:
Step 1: Eigenvalues: \[ \det\begin{pmatrix} 4 - \lambda & 1 \\ -1 & 2 - \lambda \end{pmatrix} = (4 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) + 1 = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 9 = (\lambda - 3)^2 = 0 \implies \lambda = 3 \quad \text{(multiplicity 2)}. \]

Step 2: Eigenvector: \[ (A - 3I)\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_{11} \\ v_{12} \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \implies v_{11} + v_{12} = 0 \implies \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Only one independent eigenvector exists (geometric multiplicity 1).

Step 3: Generalized eigenvector: Solve \( (A - 3I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 \): \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_{21} \\ v_{22} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \implies v_{21} + v_{22} = 1. \] Choosing \( v_{22} = 0 \implies v_{21} = 1 \), so \( \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \).

Step 4: General solution: \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = C_1 e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} + C_2 e^{3t}\left[\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + t\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\right] = e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix} C_1 + C_2(1 + t) \\ -C_1 - C_2 t \end{pmatrix}. \]
